title: Why Do We Clink Glasses Before Drinking?

fin.big: Simplified illustrations. No theory of the clink is proven.
fin.small: Sources: NPR, 'Why We Toast' (2012), quoting historian Paul Dickson; EHL Hospitality Insights, 'The origin of the toast'; Toastmaster magazine, 'A Historical Odyssey' (Dec 2018); Shakespeare, The Merry Wives of Windsor.

parts: Why do we clink glasses before we drink?
Stay for the poison story, and why even a historian of toasts can't confirm it.
Drinking to someone's health is ancient.
One historian points to Homer, where Ulysses drinks to the health of Achilles.
The word toast is stranger. People once dropped a piece of toasted bread into their wine.
Shakespeare's Falstaff orders a quart of sack and says: put a toast in it.
But the clink itself is much harder to explain than the drink.
The famous answer: the clink splashed wine between cups, so nobody dared poison you.
A hospitality school says there is no evidence for it.
And that historian's research can't confirm it either.
Other guesses: the ring scared off evil spirits, or it let your ears join in.
Our reading: every answer is still a guess. Subscribe for the next one.
